$\,,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)⟩$"] ["question-7043d5b3-b126-54ab-a0bc-9816029b7532" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the unit tangent vector $T(t).$ To do this, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{3}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(0)^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)^{2}+(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4({cos}^{2}⁡2t+{sin}^{2}⁡2t)} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the unit tangent vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}⟨0,\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal normal $N(t).$ To do this, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(0),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩ \\  & =-2⟨0,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =|-2|\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{(\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡2t+{cos}^{2}⁡2t} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${T}^{′}(t)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖} \\  & =\frac{-2⟨0,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩}{2} \\  & =⟨0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-7043d5b3-b126-54ab-a0bc-9816029b7532" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-11c25002-d570-5188-8443-f9f108b5d95d" :answer-field/id #uuid "11c25002-d570-5188-8443-f9f108b5d95d"] ["answer-ba0cef59-7cae-59d5-aee5-dae91a214aef" :answer/id #uuid "ba0cef59-7cae-59d5-aee5-dae91a214aef"] ["answer-ba0cef59-7cae-59d5-aee5-dae91a214aef" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-ba0cef59-7cae-59d5-aee5-dae91a214aef" :answer/value "-\sin(2t)"] ["answer-field-11c25002-d570-5188-8443-f9f108b5d95d" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-11c25002-d570-5188-8443-f9f108b5d95d" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-11c25002-d570-5188-8443-f9f108b5d95d" :answer-field/correct "answer-ba0cef59-7cae-59d5-aee5-dae91a214aef"] ["answer-field-11c25002-d570-5188-8443-f9f108b5d95d" :answer-field/choices "answer-ba0cef59-7cae-59d5-aee5-dae91a214aef"] ["question-7043d5b3-b126-54ab-a0bc-9816029b7532" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-11c25002-d570-5188-8443-f9f108b5d95d"] [17592186119786 :knowledge-point/questions "question-7043d5b3-b126-54ab-a0bc-9816029b7532"] ["question-bc713dbc-3c1f-5a9c-8a2b-b4377300bc92" :question/id #uuid "bc713dbc-3c1f-5a9c-8a2b-b4377300bc92"] ["question-bc713dbc-3c1f-5a9c-8a2b-b4377300bc92" :question/math-academy-id "q-75410"] ["question-bc713dbc-3c1f-5a9c-8a2b-b4377300bc92" :question/problem "The unit tangent vector to a curve at an arbitrary point is given by

$$
T(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+9}}\cdot q(t).
$$

Find the principal normal vector at the point where $t=0,$ if 

$$
\begin{aligned}q(0)=⟨0,3⟩,\,{q}^{′}(0)=⟨1,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-bc713dbc-3c1f-5a9c-8a2b-b4377300bc92" :question/worked-solution "First, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+9}}\cdot q(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+9}})\cdot q(t)+\frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+9}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(q(t)) \\  & =-\frac{t}{({t}^{2}+9)\sqrt{{t}^{2}+9}}\cdot q(t)+\frac{1}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+9}}\cdot {q}^{′}(t) \\  \\ {T}^{′}(0) & =-\frac{0}{({0}^{2}+9)\sqrt{{0}^{2}+9}}\cdot q(0)+\frac{1}{\sqrt{{0}^{2}+9}}\cdot {q}^{′}(0) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we find the magnitude of ${T}^{′}(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{T}^{′}(0)‖ & =\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}=\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${T}^{′}(0)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve at the point where $t=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}N(0) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(0)}{‖{T}^{′}(0)‖} \\  & =\frac{\frac{1}{3}⟨1,0⟩}{(\frac{1}{3})} \\  & =⟨1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Note that when we find the scalar product of $T$ and $N$ at the point where $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}T(0)\cdot N(0) & =\frac{1}{3}q(0)\cdot ⟨1,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨0,3⟩\cdot ⟨1,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(0\cdot 1+3\cdot 0) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(0+0) \\  & =0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-bc713dbc-3c1f-5a9c-8a2b-b4377300bc92" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-6e89c597-7b48-520a-9aa5-d249aa23a780" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "The unit tangent vector to a curve at an arbitrary point is given by

$$
T(t)=\frac{1}{1+3{t}^{2}}\cdot q(t).
$$

Find the principal normal vector at the point where $t=1,$ if 

$$
\begin{aligned}q(1)=⟨1,\sqrt{6},3⟩,\,{q}^{′}(1)=⟨0,\sqrt{6},6⟩.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-86bd8ee0-d1c5-5e4f-9534-8a4e93bb860c" :question/worked-solution "First, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{1+3{t}^{2}}\cdot q(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{1+3{t}^{2}})\cdot q(t)+\frac{1}{1+3{t}^{2}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(q(t)) \\  & =-\frac{6t}{{(1+3{t}^{2})}^{2}}\cdot q(t)+\frac{1}{1+3{t}^{2}}\cdot {q}^{′}(t) \\  \\ {T}^{′}(1) & =-\frac{6(1)}{{(1+3(1)^{2})}^{2}}\cdot q(1)+\frac{1}{1+3(1)^{2}}\cdot {q}^{′}(1) \\  & =-\frac{3}{8}⟨1,\sqrt{6},3⟩+\frac{1}{4}⟨0,\sqrt{6},6⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{8}(-3⟨1,\sqrt{6},3⟩+2⟨0,\sqrt{6},6⟩) \\  & =\frac{1}{8}⟨-3,-\sqrt{6},3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we find the magnitude of ${T}^{′}(1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{T}^{′}(1)‖ & =\frac{1}{8}\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+(-\sqrt{6})^{2}+{3}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\sqrt{24} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{6}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${T}^{′}(1)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve at the point where $t=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}N(0) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(1)}{‖{T}^{′}(1)‖} \\  & =\frac{\frac{1}{8}⟨-3,-\sqrt{6},3⟩}{(\frac{\sqrt{6}}{4})} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{6}}⟨-3,-\sqrt{6},3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Note that when we find the scalar product of $T$ and $N$ at the point where $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}T(1)\cdot N(1) & =\frac{1}{4}q(1)\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{6}}⟨-3,-\sqrt{6},3⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{4}⟨1,\sqrt{6},3⟩\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{6}}⟨-3,-\sqrt{6},3⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{8\sqrt{6}}(1\cdot (-3)+\sqrt{6}\cdot (-\sqrt{6})+3\cdot 3) \\  & =\frac{1}{8\sqrt{6}}(-3-6+9) \\  & =0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-86bd8ee0-d1c5-5e4f-9534-8a4e93bb860c" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-2dcaf563-74bd-51e5-bbaf-671c2387e005" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "The unit tangent vector to a curve at an arbitrary point is given by

$$
T(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+1}}\cdot q(t).
$$

Find the principal normal vector at the point where $t=0,$ if 

$$
\begin{aligned}q(0)=⟨0,1,1⟩,\,{q}^{′}(0)=⟨0,1,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-35b2b5dc-be5b-531e-92b7-e1931e890d8a" :question/worked-solution "First, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+1}}\cdot q(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+1}})\cdot q(t)+\frac{1}{\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+1}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(q(t)) \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{2t}}{({e}^{2t}+1)^{3/2}}\cdot q(t)+\frac{1}{\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+1}}\cdot {q}^{′}(t) \\  \\ {T}^{′}(0) & =-\frac{{e}^{0}}{({e}^{0}+1)^{3/2}}\cdot q(0)+\frac{1}{\sqrt{{e}^{0}+1}}\cdot {q}^{′}(0) \\  & =-\frac{1}{{2}^{3/2}}⟨0,1,1⟩+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨0,1,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{{2}^{3/2}}(-⟨0,1,1⟩+2⟨0,1,0⟩) \\  & =\frac{1}{{2}^{3/2}}⟨0,1,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we find the magnitude of ${T}^{′}(0):$

$$

- is perpendicular to the unit tangent vector, and

- points in the direction that the curve is bending.

In general, if the unit tangent vector is given by $\mathbf T(t),$ then the principal normal vector is given by

$$
\mathbf N(t)= \dfrac{\mathbf T'(t)}{\|\mathbf T'(t)\|},
$$

where it is assumed that $\|\mathbf T'(t)\|\neq 0.$

To demonstrate, suppose that the curve $C$ is parametrized by the vector function 

$$
\mathbf f(t) = \left\langle 2\cos t, \: 2\sin t \right\rangle, \qquad t \in [0, \pi].
$$

We will compute the principal normal vector at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}.$

First, using the formula for the unit tangent, $\mathbf T(t) = \dfrac{\mathbf f'(t)}{||\mathbf f'(t)||},$ we find that the general unit tangent vector is

$$
\mathbf T(t)= \left\langle {-\sin t}, \cos t\right\rangle.
$$

Now, when $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4},$ we have the point $P(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2}).$ The unit tangent vector $\mathbf{T}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$ and the principal normal vector $\mathbf{N}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$ at this point are shown below:

![](images/d0/d0a30a44bb825a8a12ca54153b6223b9bf0c2b754245b21650a5664db5e1647e.png)

To calculate the principal normal vector, we start by calculating the derivative of the unit tangent function. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ {T}^{′}(t) & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general principal normal vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{||{T}^{′}(t)||} \\  & =\frac{⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩}{\sqrt{(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩}{\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}} \\  & =\frac{⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩}{\sqrt{1}} \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now find $\mathbf N\left(\dfrac\pi 4\right),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}),\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, it's easy to check that $\mathbf T'(t)$ and $\mathbf N'(t)$ are perpendicular for all $t$ by computing the dot product and showing that we get zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t)\cdot N(t) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\cdot ⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186121149 :tutorial/content "Let $\mathbf T(t)$ be the unit tangent vector to some differentiable vector-valued function. Since $||\mathbf T(t)|| = 1,$ and $\mathbf T(t)$ is obviously parallel to itself, we must have

$$
\mathbf T(t) \cdot \mathbf T(t) = 1.
$$

Differentiating the above relationship with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\mathbf T'(t) \cdot \mathbf T(t) + \mathbf T(t) \cdot \mathbf T'(t) = 0,
$$

which can be simplified as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t)\cdot T(t)+{T}^{′}(t)\cdot T(t) & =0 \\ 2{T}^{′}(t)\cdot T(t) & =0 \\ {T}^{′}(t)\cdot T(t) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, provided that $\mathbf T'(t)\neq \mathbf 0,$ then it must be the case that $\mathbf T'(t)$ is perpendicular to $\mathbf T(t).$

The vector $\mathbf T'(t)$ measures the rate of change of $\mathbf T(t).$ However, since $\mathbf T(t)$ is a unit vector for all $t,$ it changes only in its direction. The vector $\mathbf T'(t)$ measures this rate of change in direction.

\begin{aligned}r(t) & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+t\,[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0 \\ \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

 

If we attempt to calculate its principal normal vector, we will get an interesting result. First, we calculate $\mathbf r'(t)$ and $\|\mathbf r'(t)\|
\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[\begin{aligned}-2+5t \\ 1 \\ \sqrt{2}t\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0 \\ \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}] \\ ‖{r}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{5}^{2}+(\sqrt{2})^{2}}=\sqrt{27}=3\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the unit tangent vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{{r}^{'}(t)}{‖{r}^{'}(t)‖}=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}\,[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0 \\ \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in the case of a straight line, $\mathbf T(t)$ is simply the (normalized) direction vector, as we would expect. 

Next, we calculate $\mathbf T'(t)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{'}(t) & =\frac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}\,[\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(0) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2})\end{aligned}]=0\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\mathbf{T}'(t)$ is the zero vector, we can't normalize it as usual. If we try to apply the usual formula we get an undefined result due to division by zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{'}(t)}{‖{T}^{'}(t)‖}=\frac{0}{‖0‖}=\frac{0}{0}=\text{undefined}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a straight line does not have a principal normal.

The intuition behind this result is that the principal normal points in the direction in which a curve is bending, but a straight line does not bend at all."] [17592186120641 :step/math-academy-id 164579] [17592186120642 :step/math-academy-id 164580] [17592186120643 :step/math-academy-id 164583] [17592186120644 :step/math-academy-id 164586] [17592186120645 :step/math-academy-id 164587] [17592186120646 :step/math-academy-id 164590]]}

17592186119785 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "930466fc-c7fe-51a5-8634-818abddd0da9" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Principal Normal at a Given Point"}] :question/problem "The unit tangent vector to a curve at an arbitrary point is given by

$$
\mathbf T(t) =\sin{t} \,\mathbf i -\cos{t}\,\mathbf j.
$$

Find the principal normal vector at the point where $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}.$" :question/worked-solution "Remember that in general, the principal normal vector is given by

$$
\mathbf N(t)= \dfrac{\mathbf T'(t)}{\|\mathbf T'(t)\|}.
$$

First, we calculate $\mathbf T'(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j \\ {T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,j \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,i+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,j \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we find the magnitude of $\mathbf T'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})‖ & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}‖i+j‖ \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\sqrt{{(1)}^{2}+{(1)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\sqrt{2} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $\mathbf T'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$ and obtain the principal normal vector to the curve at the point where $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}N(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})}{‖{T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})‖}=\frac{\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i+j)}{1}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,i+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

To check our result, we can verify that $\mathbf T$ and $\mathbf N$ are perpendicular by computing their dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(\frac{\pi }{4})\cdot N(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,i-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,j)\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,i+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,j) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2} \\  & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050685} {:db/id 17592186120242 :question/id #uuid "fee02912-87a3-5a99-92ba-f8ae9f270c88" :question/math-academy-id "q-33233" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186119785 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "930466fc-c7fe-51a5-8634-818abddd0da9" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Principal Normal at a Given Point"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a874d8e3-9a22-519e-9812-7190479ca678" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{3}{5}i - Find the principal normal vector to that curve at the point $P(0,3,4).$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k,\,t\in [0,2\pi ) \\ T(t) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k,\,t\in [0,2\pi )\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to the point $P(0,3,4)$ on the given curve. We know that:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨0,3,4⟩ \\ 5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k & =0\text{ }i+3\text{ }j+4\text{ }k\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components of $i$, $j$, and $k$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}5\operatorname{cos}⁡t=0 \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡t=3 \\ 4\operatorname{sin}⁡t=4\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equality, $t=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(0,3,4)$ is at the tip of the vector $r(\frac{\pi }{2}).$ 

Now, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\frac{\pi }{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,k \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j-\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k \\ {T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{2}\,i-\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2}\,j-\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2}\,k \\  & =-\frac{3}{5}\,j-\frac{4}{5}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the magnitude of ${T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})‖ & =\sqrt{(0)^{2}+{(-\frac{3}{5})}^{2}+{(-\frac{4}{5})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{9}{25}+\frac{16}{25}} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve $r(t)$ at the point $P(0,3,4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})}{‖{T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})‖}=\frac{-\frac{3}{5}\,j-\frac{4}{5}\,k}{1}=-\frac{3}{5}\,j-\frac{4}{5}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Note that when we find the scalar product of $T$ and $N$ at the point where at $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}T(\frac{\pi }{2})\cdot N(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =(-i)\cdot (-\frac{3}{5}\,j-\frac{4}{5}\,k) \\  & =\frac{3}{5}(i\cdot j)+\frac{4}{5}(i\cdot k) \\  & =0.\,✓\end{aligned}

$$

"Remember that in general, the principal normal vector is given by

$$
\mathbf N(t)= \dfrac{\mathbf T'(t)}{\|\mathbf T'(t)\|}.
$$

First, we find the unit tangent vector $\mathbf T(t).$ To do this, we calculate $\mathbf r'(t)$ and its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{3}t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\sqrt{3},\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(\sqrt{3})^{2}+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{3+{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the unit tangent vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}⟨\sqrt{3},\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},\,-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{2},\,\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal normal $\mathbf{N}(t).$ To do this, we calculate $\mathbf T'(t)$ and its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{2}⟨0,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $\mathbf T'(t)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{\frac{1}{2}⟨0,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩}{(\frac{1}{2})}=⟨0,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

To check our result, we can verify that $\mathbf T$ and $\mathbf N$ are perpendicular by computing their dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t)\cdot N(t) & =⟨\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},\,-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{2},\,\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{2}⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot 0+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{2}-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{2} \\  & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186120163 :question/id #uuid "3c19ac1e-dfbc-5900-a164-de8fb9c9dca3" :question/math-academy-id "q-222843"} {:db/id 17592186120164 :question/id #uuid "bbe7871a-ccc9-5a95-8370-21299423ec38" :question/math-academy-id "q-222851" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186119786 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "8d21e1c3-1529-5471-a1e6-76f174da79c3" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Principal Normal at an Arbitrary Point"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9455b7e1-8e45-5b8d-8930-b09294afde81" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\operatorname{sin}t" :db/id 17592186289026}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "9455b7e1-8e45-5b8d-8930-b09294afde81" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\operatorname{sin}t" :db/id 17592186289026} :answer-field/id #uuid "b860cd5e-c7b3-588c-8a3f-8511ad544821" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186290133}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Given  the curve $r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,4t⟩$, find the principal normal vector $N(t)$ at an arbitrary point on the curve.

\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(4)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)+16} \\  & =\sqrt{25} \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the unit tangent vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\frac{4}{5}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal normal $N(t).$ To do this, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{4}{5})⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{3}{5}⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,0⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(-\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{9}{25}({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${T}^{′}(t)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{\frac{3}{5}⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,0⟩}{(\frac{3}{5})}=⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,0⟩\end{aligned}

$$
\mathbf T(t) = \sin{t} \cdot \mathbf q(t).
$$

Find the principal normal vector at the point where $t = \dfrac{\pi}{4},$ if 

$$
\begin{aligned}q(\frac{\pi }{4})=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,i-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,j+k,\,{q}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})=-2\,k.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Remember that in general, the principal normal vector is given by

$$
\mathbf N(t)= \dfrac{\mathbf T'(t)}{\|\mathbf T'(t)\|}.
$$

First, we calculate $\mathbf T'(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot q(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot q(t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(q(t)) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot q(t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot {q}^{′}(t) \\  \\ {T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\cdot q(\frac{\pi }{4})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\cdot {q}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,i-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,j+k)+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(-2\,k) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\,i-\frac{1}{2}\,j-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we find the magnitude of $\mathbf T'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})‖ & =\sqrt{{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{2}} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $\mathbf T'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve at the point where $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}N(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})}{‖{T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})‖} \\  & =\frac{-\frac{1}{2}\,i-\frac{1}{2}\,j-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,k}{1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\,i-\frac{1}{2}\,j-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,k\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186120520 :question/id #uuid "7ee0cbfa-763d-5927-b2fe-7883ea79f8f3" :question/math-academy-id "q-74864" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186119787 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "01fe665f-05e8-5183-9c98-cb760af0ae02" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating a Principal Normal Given Some Information About a Curve"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "826649c3-ffe7-5f54-9966-eebc83615bcf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-j" :db/id 17592186119235} {:answer/id #uuid "8616fccd-bcb5-58e3-ba7b-e4f994cec92c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}i + \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}j" :db/id 17592186119236} {:answer/id #uuid "af7b3031-a20c-5778-a8d4-9072e940f52f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}i - \frac{2\sqrt{5}}{5}j" :db/id 17592186119237} {:answer/id #uuid "f695d4cc-4d27-5342-b366-23348b8d74b4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}i + \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}j" :db/id 17592186119238} {:answer/id #uuid "030380d0-84f6-5258-88d6-58f0ec8a168f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "i + j" :db/id 17592186119239}] :answer-field/id #uuid "74e24ea7-f7a1-5490-a29b-1f9c2dc00269" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186119234}] :question/problem "The unit tangent vector to a curve at an arbitrary point is given by

:question/problem "The unit tangent vector to a curve at an arbitrary point is given by

$$
T(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+4t}}\cdot q(t).
$$

Find the principal normal vector at the point where $t=2,$ if 

$$
\begin{aligned}q(2)=⟨1,2\sqrt{2}⟩,\,{q}^{′}(2)=⟨0,\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+4t}}\cdot q(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+4t}})\cdot q(t)+\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+4t}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(q(t)) \\  & =-\frac{2}{(1+4t)^{3/2}}\cdot q(t)+\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+4t}}\cdot {q}^{′}(t) \\  \\ {T}^{′}(2) & =-\frac{2}{(1+4(2))^{3/2}}\cdot q(2)+\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+4(2)}}\cdot {q}^{′}(2) \\  & =-\frac{2}{27}⟨1,2\sqrt{2}⟩+\frac{1}{3}⟨0,\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{27}(-2⟨1,2\sqrt{2}⟩+9⟨0,\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟩) \\  & =\frac{1}{27}⟨-2,\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{54}⟨-4,\sqrt{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we find the magnitude of ${T}^{′}(2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{T}^{′}(2)‖ & =\frac{1}{54}\sqrt{(-4)^{2}+(\sqrt{2})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{54}\cdot \sqrt{18} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{18}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${T}^{′}(2)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve at the point where $t=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}N(2) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(2)}{‖{T}^{′}(2)‖} \\  & =\frac{\frac{1}{54}⟨-4,\sqrt{2}⟩}{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{18})} \\  & =\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}⟨-4,\sqrt{2}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨-2\sqrt{2},1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Note that when we find the scalar product of $T$ and $N$ at the point where $t=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}T(2)\cdot N(2) & =\frac{1}{3}q(2)\cdot \frac{1}{3}⟨-2\sqrt{2},1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨1,2\sqrt{2}⟩\cdot \frac{1}{3}⟨-2\sqrt{2},1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{9}(1\cdot (-2\sqrt{2})+2\sqrt{2}\cdot 1) \\  & =\frac{1}{9}(-2\sqrt{2}+2\sqrt{2}) \\  & =0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186345083 :question/id #uuid "e872eb2a-80c0-5fe7-b915-1fedf1110b20" :question/math-academy-id "q-75407"} {:db/id 17592186345091 :question/id #uuid :topic/math-academy-id 1795} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186120641 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121148 :tutorial/content "The **principal normal vector** to a curve $C$ at a point $P$ is a unit vector that 

- is perpendicular to the unit tangent vector, and

- points in the direction that the curve is bending.

In general, if the unit tangent vector is given by $\mathbf T(t),$ then the principal normal vector is given by

$$
\mathbf N(t)= \dfrac{\mathbf T'(t)}{\|\mathbf T'(t)\|},
$$

where it is assumed that $\|\mathbf T'(t)\|\neq 0.$

To demonstrate, suppose that the curve $C$ is parametrized by the vector function 

$$
\mathbf f(t) = \left\langle 2\cos t, \: 2\sin t \right\rangle, \qquad t \in [0, \pi].
$$

We will compute the principal normal vector at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}.$

First, using the formula for the unit tangent, $\mathbf T(t) = \dfrac{\mathbf f'(t)}{||\mathbf f'(t)||},$ we find that the general unit tangent vector is

$$
\mathbf T(t)= \left\langle {-\sin t}, \cos t\right\rangle.
$$

Now, when $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4},$ we have the point $P(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2}).$ The unit tangent vector $\mathbf{T}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$ and the principal normal vector $\mathbf{N}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$ at this point are shown below:

![](images/d0/d0a30a44bb825a8a12ca54153b6223b9bf0c2b754245b21650a5664db5e1647e.png)

To calculate the principal normal vector, we start by calculating the derivative of the unit tangent function. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}t,\operatorname{cos}t⟩ \\ {T}^{'}(t) & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}t,\,-\operatorname{sin}t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general principal normal vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{'}(t)}{||{T}^{'}(t)||} \\  & =\frac{⟨-\operatorname{cos}t,\,-\operatorname{sin}t⟩}{\sqrt{(-\operatorname{cos}t)^{2}+(\operatorname{sin}t)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{⟨-\operatorname{cos}t,\,-\operatorname{sin}t⟩}{\sqrt{{cos}^{2}t+{sin}^{2}t}} \\  & =\frac{⟨-\operatorname{cos}t,\,-\operatorname{sin}t⟩}{\sqrt{1}} \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}t,\,-\operatorname{sin}t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now find $\mathbf N\left(\dfrac\pi 4\right),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}(\frac{\pi }{4}),\,-\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{4})⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, it's easy to check that $\mathbf T'(t)$ and $\mathbf N'(t)$ are perpendicular for all $t$ by computing the dot product and showing that we get zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t)\cdot N(t) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}t,\operatorname{cos}t⟩\cdot ⟨-\operatorname{cos}t,\,-\operatorname{sin}t⟩ \\  & =\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t-\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t \\  & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "03709847-4a63-5975-b20a-1d6693ceadb3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9376 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "c3443d00-c515-5a63-93a0-747d76d2271c" :step/math-academy-id 164579 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120642}} {:db/id 17592186120642 :step/content {:db/id 17592186119785 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119532 :question/id #uuid "8cb590c5-586d-56a1-af70-d693ea055419" :question/math-academy-id "e-14996"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "930466fc-c7fe-51a5-8634-818abddd0da9" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050685}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186120242} {:db/id 17592186120252} {:db/id 17592186262761} {:db/id 17592186311553} {:db/id 17592186344986} {:db/id 17592186398305}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Principal Normal at a Given Point"} :step/id #uuid "c9c3f801-f35a-5089-8d66-01d0fd9903d2" :step/math-academy-id 164580 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120643}} {:db/id 17592186120643 :step/content {:db/id 17592186119786 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119533 :question/id #uuid "2f92f568-0bf5-58bd-87ce-e6be8d05fe69" :question/math-academy-id "e-14997"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "8d21e1c3-1529-5471-a1e6-76f174da79c3" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186120163} {:db/id 17592186120164} {:db/id 17592186290398} {:db/id 17592186290399} {:db/id 17592186290400} {:db/id 17592186290401} {:db/id 17592186290402} {:db/id 17592186323724} {:db/id 17592186323725}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Principal Normal at an Arbitrary Point"} :step/id #uuid "812571c6-b194-5ab1-b16a-bcf2ac6ffbe9" :step/math-academy-id 164583 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120644}} {:db/id 17592186120644 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121149 :tutorial/content "Let $\mathbf T(t)$ be the unit tangent vector to some differentiable vector-valued function. Since $||\mathbf T(t)|| = 1,$ and $\mathbf T(t)$ is obviously parallel to itself, we must have

$$
\mathbf T(t) \cdot \mathbf T(t) = 1.
$$

Differentiating the above relationship with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\mathbf T'(t) \cdot \mathbf T(t) + \mathbf T(t) \cdot \mathbf T'(t) = 0,
$$

which can be simplified as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{'}(t)\cdot T(t)+{T}^{'}(t)\cdot T(t) & =0 \\ 2{T}^{'}(t)\cdot T(t) & =0 \\ {T}^{'}(t)\cdot T(t) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, provided that $\mathbf T'(t)\neq \mathbf 0,$ then it must be the case that $\mathbf T'(t)$ is perpendicular to $\mathbf T(t).$

The vector $\mathbf T'(t)$ measures the rate of change of $\mathbf T(t).$ However, since $\mathbf T(t)$ is a unit vector for all $t,$ it changes only in its direction. The vector $\mathbf T'(t)$ measures this rate of change in direction. 

To form the principal normal $\mathbf N(t),$ we normalize $\mathbf T'(t),$ which leads to the definition

$$
\mathbf N(t) = \dfrac{\mathbf T'(t)}{||\mathbf T'(t)||}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "bd9190b9-f59c-5c06-987a-c6269ec9b3a7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9377 :tutorial/title "Deriving the Formula for the Principal Normal"} :step/id #uuid "ee849a7a-e449-5317-872e-183c46fabb72" :step/math-academy-id 164586 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120645}} {:db/id 17592186120645 :step/content {:db/id 17592186119787 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119534 :question/id #uuid "f5e6498b-73f9-5760-81bb-14e9acc495f8" :question/math-academy-id "e-14998"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "01fe665f-05e8-5183-9c98-cb760af0ae02" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186120520} {:db/id 17592186120521} {:db/id 17592186262795} {:db/id 17592186262799} {:db/id 17592186345083} {:db/id 17592186345091} {:db/id 17592186398312} {:db/id 17592186398319} {:db/id 17592186398326}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating a Principal Normal Given Some Information About a Curve"} :step/id #uuid "8e583ccb-952c-52c6-b8a9-e4b716f0d3c4" :step/math-academy-id 164587 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120646}} {:db/id 17592186120646 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121150 :tutorial/content "Consider the straight line given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+t\,[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0 \\ \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

 

If we attempt to calculate its principal normal vector, we will get an interesting result. First, we calculate $\mathbf r'(t)$ and $\|\mathbf r'(t)\|
\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[\begin{aligned}-2+5t \\ 1 \\ \sqrt{2}t\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0 \\ \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}] \\ ‖{r}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{5}^{2}+(\sqrt{2})^{2}}=\sqrt{27}=3\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the unit tangent vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{{r}^{'}(t)}{‖{r}^{'}(t)‖}=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}\,[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0 \\ \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in the case of a straight line, $\mathbf T(t)$ is simply the (normalized) direction vector, as we would expect. 

Next, we calculate $\mathbf T'(t)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{'}(t) & =\frac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}\,[\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(0) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2})\end{aligned}]=0\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\mathbf{T}'(t)$ is the zero vector, we can't normalize it as usual. If we try to apply the usual formula we get an undefined result due to division by zero:

$$

The intuition behind this result is that the principal normal points in the direction in which a curve is bending, but a straight line does not bend at all." :tutorial/id #uuid "5c27df4b-0d17-5407-997b-c240d492eeca" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9378 :tutorial/title "Lines Do Not Have Principal Normal Vectors"} :step/id #uuid "1aa2d247-5dd4-5fdf-a44a-9cf0a8cd1e0d" :step/math-academy-id 164590}] :activity/title "Principal Normal Vectors" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186120013} {:db/id 17592186120641 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121148 :tutorial/content "The **principal normal vector** to a curve $C$ at a point $P$ is a unit vector that 

- is perpendicular to the unit tangent vector, and

- points in the direction that the curve is bending.

In general, if the unit tangent vector is given by $\mathbf T(t),$ then the principal normal vector is given by

$$
\mathbf N(t)= \dfrac{\mathbf T'(t)}{\|\mathbf T'(t)\|},
$$

where it is assumed that $\|\mathbf T'(t)\|\neq 0.$

To demonstrate, suppose that the curve $C$ is parametrized by the vector function 

$$
\mathbf f(t) = \left\langle 2\cos t, \: 2\sin t \right\rangle, \qquad t \in [0, \pi].
$$

We will compute the principal normal vector at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}.$

First, using the formula for the unit tangent, $\mathbf T(t) = \dfrac{\mathbf f'(t)}{||\mathbf f'(t)||},$ we find that the general unit tangent vector is

$$
\mathbf T(t)= \left\langle {-\sin t}, \cos t\right\rangle.
$$

Now, when $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4},$ we have the point $P(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2}).$ The unit tangent vector $\mathbf{T}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$ and the principal normal vector $\mathbf{N}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$ at this point are shown below:

![](images/d0/d0a30a44bb825a8a12ca54153b6223b9bf0c2b754245b21650a5664db5e1647e.png)

To calculate the principal normal vector, we start by calculating the derivative of the unit tangent function. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}t,\operatorname{cos}t⟩ \\ {T}^{'}(t) & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}t,\,-\operatorname{sin}t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general principal normal vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{'}(t)}{||{T}^{'}(t)||} \\  & =\frac{⟨-\operatorname{cos}t,\,-\operatorname{sin}t⟩}{\sqrt{(-\operatorname{cos}t)^{2}+(\operatorname{sin}t)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{⟨-\operatorname{cos}t,\,-\operatorname{sin}t⟩}{\sqrt{{cos}^{2}t+{sin}^{2}t}} \\  & =\frac{⟨-\operatorname{cos}t,\,-\operatorname{sin}t⟩}{\sqrt{1}} \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}t,\,-\operatorname{sin}t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now find $\mathbf N\left(\dfrac\pi 4\right),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}(\frac{\pi }{4}),\,-\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{4})⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, it's easy to check that $\mathbf T'(t)$ and $\mathbf N'(t)$ are perpendicular for all $t$ by computing the dot product and showing that we get zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t)\cdot N(t) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}t,\operatorname{cos}t⟩\cdot ⟨-\operatorname{cos}t,\,-\operatorname{sin}t⟩ \\  & =\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t-\operatorname{sin}t\operatorname{cos}t \\  & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "03709847-4a63-5975-b20a-1d6693ceadb3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9376 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "c3443d00-c515-5a63-93a0-747d76d2271c" :step/math-academy-id 164579 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120642}} {:db/id 17592186121148 :tutorial/content "The **principal normal vector** to a curve $C$ at a point $P$ is a unit vector that

Since $||\mathbf T(t)|| = 1,$ and $\mathbf T(t)$ is obviously parallel to itself, we must have

$$
\mathbf T(t) \cdot \mathbf T(t) = 1.
$$

Differentiating the above relationship with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\mathbf T'(t) \cdot \mathbf T(t) + \mathbf T(t) \cdot \mathbf T'(t) = 0,
$$

which can be simplified as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{'}(t)\cdot T(t)+{T}^{'}(t)\cdot T(t) & =0 \\ 2{T}^{'}(t)\cdot T(t) & =0 \\ {T}^{'}(t)\cdot T(t) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, provided that $\mathbf T'(t)\neq \mathbf 0,$ then it must be the case that $\mathbf T'(t)$ is perpendicular to $\mathbf T(t).$

The vector $\mathbf T'(t)$ measures the rate of change of $\mathbf T(t).$ However, since $\mathbf T(t)$ is a unit vector for all $t,$ it changes only in its direction. The vector $\mathbf T'(t)$ measures this rate of change in direction. 

To form the principal normal $\mathbf N(t),$ we normalize $\mathbf T'(t),$ which leads to the definition

$$
\mathbf N(t) = \dfrac{\mathbf T'(t)}{||\mathbf T'(t)||}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "bd9190b9-f59c-5c06-987a-c6269ec9b3a7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9377 :tutorial/title "Deriving the Formula for the Principal Normal"} :step/id #uuid "ee849a7a-e449-5317-872e-183c46fabb72" :step/math-academy-id 164586 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120645}} {:db/id 17592186121149 :tutorial/content "Let $\mathbf T(t)$ be the unit tangent vector to some differentiable vector-valued function. $$

$$
\mathbf T'(t) \cdot \mathbf T(t) + \mathbf T(t) \cdot \mathbf T'(t) = 0,
$$

which can be simplified as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{'}(t)\cdot T(t)+{T}^{'}(t)\cdot T(t) & =0 \\ 2{T}^{'}(t)\cdot T(t) & =0 \\ {T}^{'}(t)\cdot T(t) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, provided that $\mathbf T'(t)\neq \mathbf 0,$ then it must be the case that $\mathbf T'(t)$ is perpendicular to $\mathbf T(t).$

The vector $\mathbf T'(t)$ measures the rate of change of $\mathbf T(t).$ However, since $\mathbf T(t)$ is a unit vector for all $t,$ it changes only in its direction. The vector $\mathbf T'(t)$ measures this rate of change in direction. 

To form the principal normal $\mathbf N(t),$ we normalize $\mathbf T'(t),$ which leads to the definition

$$
\mathbf N(t) = \dfrac{\mathbf T'(t)}{||\mathbf T'(t)||}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "bd9190b9-f59c-5c06-987a-c6269ec9b3a7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9377 :tutorial/title "Deriving the Formula for the Principal Normal"} {:db/id 17592186120645 :step/content {:db/id 17592186119787 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119534 :question/id #uuid "f5e6498b-73f9-5760-81bb-14e9acc495f8" :question/math-academy-id "e-14998"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "01fe665f-05e8-5183-9c98-cb760af0ae02" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186120520} {:db/id 17592186120521} {:db/id 17592186262795} {:db/id 17592186262799} {:db/id 17592186345083} {:db/id 17592186345091} {:db/id 17592186398312} {:db/id 17592186398319} {:db/id 17592186398326}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating a Principal Normal Given Some Information About a Curve"} :step/id #uuid "8e583ccb-952c-52c6-b8a9-e4b716f0d3c4" :step/math-academy-id 164587 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120646}} {:db/id 17592186120646 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121150 :tutorial/content "Consider the straight line given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+t\,[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0 \\ \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

 

If we attempt to calculate its principal normal vector, we will get an interesting result. First, we calculate $\mathbf r'(t)$ and $\|\mathbf r'(t)\|
\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[\begin{aligned}-2+5t \\ 1 \\ \sqrt{2}t\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0 \\ \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}] \\ ‖{r}^{'}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{5}^{2}+(\sqrt{2})^{2}}=\sqrt{27}=3\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the unit tangent vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{{r}^{'}(t)}{‖{r}^{'}(t)‖}=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}\,[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0 \\ \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in the case of a straight line, $\mathbf T(t)$ is simply the (normalized) direction vector, as we would expect. 

Next, we calculate $\mathbf T'(t)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{'}(t) & =\frac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}\,[\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(0) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2})\end{aligned}]=0\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\mathbf{T}'(t)$ is the zero vector, we can't normalize it as usual. If we try to apply the usual formula we get an undefined result due to division by zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{'}(t)}{‖{T}^{'}(t)‖}=\frac{0}{‖0‖}=\frac{0}{0}=\text{undefined}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a straight line does not have a principal normal.

17592186045417] [17592186046659 1007 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences I" 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1008 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences I develops the core mathematical structures and analytical tools used throughout theoretical and applied physics. Building on calculus and introductory linear algebra, the course introduces vector geometry, multivariable analysis, and differential equations in a unified framework designed for modeling physical systems.
Students learn how mathematical concepts such as vector spaces, linear transformations, multivariable functions, and differential equations provide the language and computational techniques used to describe motion, fields, and dynamical processes. The course emphasizes connections between abstract mathematical ideas and the physical principles they support, preparing students for advanced study in classical mechanics, electromagnetism, and related areas of physics." 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics that support later mathematical modeling in physics. Students study vector geometry in three-dimensional space, including equations of lines and planes and geometric relationships between them. These tools appear naturally in the description of trajectories, rays, and intersections of physical surfaces. Introductory set theory provides a precise language for describing mathematical structures and regions in space, supporting later work in multivariable analysis and probability.
Students then develop computational tools from linear algebra. Methods such as Gaussian elimination, matrix inverses, determinants, and LU factorization are used to analyze and solve systems of linear equations. These techniques arise when solving coupled equations in physical models, such as electrical circuits, mechanical systems with multiple interacting components, and discretized approximations of physical fields.
The course next develops the structure of vector spaces and linear transformations. Students study spans, bases, dimension, rank, and null spaces, and extend these ideas to abstract vector spaces. Linear maps and their matrix representations are examined, establishing the connection between geometric transformations and matrix algebra. These ideas culminate in the study of eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and matrix diagonalization, which are central tools for solving differential equations describing oscillations, normal modes of vibration, and stability of dynamical systems.
The course then turns to multivariable calculus and vector analysis. Students analyze functions of several variables, quadric surfaces, and coordinate transformations. Partial derivatives, gradients, and the multivariable chain rule are developed along with linear approximations and higher-order derivatives. These concepts describe how physical quantities such as temperature, pressure, or electric potential vary in space. Vector-valued functions and vector fields are studied together with curvature, divergence, and curl, providing the mathematical language used to describe velocity fields in fluid flow and electric and magnetic fields in electromagnetism.
Students then study multiple integration, focusing on double integrals and coordinate transformations such as polar coordinates. These techniques allow the computation of physical quantities distributed over regions, such as mass, charge, or probability density.
The final portion of the course introduces differential equations as models of dynamical systems. Students study first-order equations and qualitative behavior of solutions through phase-line analysis. Applications include motion under drag, gravitational attraction, electrical circuits, and population dynamics.
